title: Authentication vs. authorization, JWT and OAuth2
summary: Authentication answers "who are you?" (401 if it fails).

sections.definition: Authentication answers "who are you?" (401 if it fails). Authorization answers "may you do this?" (403 if it fails). The most common mechanisms are Basic, API keys, cookie sessions, JWT with refresh tokens and OAuth2 to delegate access.
sections.analogy: At a hotel, the front desk checks your ID and gives you a key card (authentication). The card opens your room and the gym, but not the presidential suite (authorization). The card stops working on checkout day (expiration). OAuth2 is giving the laundry service a limited card that only opens your closet, without handing over yours.
sections.problem: A JWT has three parts: the header (algorithm), the payload (claims such as sub, role, exp) and the signature, which guarantees nobody modified the first two. Since it cannot be revoked easily, the access token is short-lived (5–15 min) and a long-lived refresh token, stored securely and revocable on the server, is used to request a new one.
sections.code:wire:
# Basic: usuario:clave en Base64 (no es cifrado). Solo sobre HTTPS.
Authorization: Basic YW5hOnNlY3JldG8=

# API key: identifica a una aplicación, no a una persona
X-API-Key: sk_live_9f2c...

# JWT = header.payload.firma (Base64URL)
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJzdWIiOiI3Iiwicm9sZSI6ImNsaWVudGUiLCJleHAiOjE3OTk5OTk5OTl9.Xb3...

# Renovación con refresh token
POST /v1/auth/refresh
Cookie: refresh=rt_8c1f...; HttpOnly; Secure
→ 200 {"access_token":"eyJ... (nuevo, 15 min)"}
sections.code:server:
import jwt   # PyJWT
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

def crear_access_token(usuario_id: int, rol: str) -> str:
    payload = {"sub": str(usuario_id), "role": rol,
               "exp": datetime.now(timezone.utc) + timedelta(minutes=15)}
    return jwt.encode(payload, SECRET, algorithm="HS256")

def usuario_actual(token: str = Depends(oauth2)):
    try:
        datos = jwt.decode(token, SECRET, algorithms=["HS256"])  # valida firma y exp
    except jwt.PyJWTError:
        raise HTTPException(401, headers={"WWW-Authenticate": "Bearer"})
    return datos

def requiere_admin(u = Depends(usuario_actual)):
    if u["role"] != "admin":
        raise HTTPException(403)   # autorización
    return u

# Guardar datos sensibles en el payload y confiar en el rol que manda el cliente
{"sub":"7","role":"admin","password":"secreto"}   ← cualquiera lo lee
jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False})   ← acepta tokens falsificados
sections.good:
# Payload mínimo, firma verificada, expiración corta, algoritmo fijado
jwt.decode(token, SECRET, algorithms=["HS256"])
sections.bridge:typescript: Your own function that wraps fetch and, on a 401, calls /refresh and retries the original request is the client half of the refresh token flow. On the server side, that 401 appears when jwt.decode detects that exp has already passed. And when you log in with Google in an app, the backend is acting as an OAuth2 client.
sections.interview: Authentication is verifying identity, and if it fails a 401 applies; authorization is deciding whether that identity may perform an action, and if it fails it is 403. Basic sends username and password in Base64 and is only acceptable over HTTPS; API keys identify applications; sessions keep the state on the server with a cookie; and a JWT is a signed token with header, payload and signature, which the server validates without querying the database, by checking signature and expiration. Since a JWT is hard to revoke, short access tokens and long, revocable refresh tokens are used. OAuth2 is a framework for an application to get limited access to a user’s resources without knowing their password; the recommended flow for web apps is Authorization Code with PKCE.
sections.myths:
• Believing OAuth2 is an authentication protocol. It is for delegated authorization; authentication on top is added by OpenID Connect (the id_token).
  • Thinking Base64 is encryption. Basic and the JWT payload are decoded in a second.
  • Validating the role only in the frontend. Hiding a button does not protect the endpoint.

exercises.prompt: Which status code does this case return?

items.q: A token with a valid signature but with exp in the past reaches your API.
items.why: The token no longer proves identity: 401. The client must use the refresh token.

items.q: A user with role "customer" calls DELETE /v1/productos/42, which requires the admin role.
items.why: They are authenticated, but not authorized: 403.
